title: Quantifiers: much, many, a lot of, a little, a few
grammarNote: Quantifiers выражают КОЛИЧЕСТВО. Главный выбор: слово СЧЁТНОЕ или НЕСЧЁТНОЕ? Яйца (eggs) можно посчитать: одно, два, три → COUNTABLE. Мука (flour) нельзя посчитать: нельзя сказать "одна мука, две муки" → UNCOUNTABLE. От этого зависит, какой quantifier используется.

grammarTable.subject: much
grammarTable.example: "How much water?" / "There isn't much time." (NOT in positive: ✗ "There is much water.")

grammarTable.subject: many
grammarTable.example: "How many eggs?" / "There aren't many students." (NOT normally in positive)

grammarTable.subject: a lot of
grammarTable.example: "There's a lot of flour." / "We need a lot of eggs." (both C and UC)

grammarTable.subject: lots of
grammarTable.example: "Lots of vegetables." / "Lots of time." (spoken English, both types)

grammarTable.subject: a little
grammarTable.example: "Add a little salt." / "She has a little money left." (UC, positive)

grammarTable.subject: a few
grammarTable.example: "Add a few tablespoons." / "I have a few friends here." (C, positive)

grammarTable.subject: some
grammarTable.example: "Have some soup." / "Could I have some water?" (positive, offers)

grammarTable.subject: any
grammarTable.example: "There isn't any milk." / "Do you have any eggs?" (negative/question)

grammarExtra.title: Countable vs Uncountable — key food examples

rows.example: eggs, carrots, apples, onions, potatoes, lentils, biscuits, sandwiches
flour, water, oil, milk, rice, salt, sugar, bread, meat, cheese, pasta
"I'd like some chicken." (UC) / "I ordered a chicken." (one whole bird — C)
One egg ✓ (C) / One flour ✗ → flour is UC

grammarExtra.title: much and many — mostly negative and question

rows.example: "I don't have much time." / "There isn't much oil." ✅
"We don't have many eggs." / "There aren't many shops open." ✅
"How many onions?" / "How many students are there?" ✅
✗ "I have much money." → ✅ "I have a lot of money." (positive = use a lot of)

grammarExtra.title: a little vs a few — small positive amounts

rows.example: "Add a little salt." / "I have a little money left." (positive and useful amount)
"Add a few drops of oil." / "I have a few friends here." (positive and useful)
"There's little hope." = very little, nearly none (negative meaning, no "a")
"Few students came." = very few, almost none (negative meaning, no "a")

grammarExtra.title: some and any — offers, positive, negative, questions

rows.example: "I have some eggs." / "She has some money." (positive)
"Would you like some tea?" / "Can I have some water?" (polite offer/request)
"I don't have any eggs." / "There isn't any milk." (negative)
"Do you have any flour?" / "Is there any bread?" (question)

grammarTip:
Главное правило quantifiers:
① COUNTABLE (можно считать: egg → eggs) → many, a few, how many
② UNCOUNTABLE (нельзя считать: flour, oil) → much, a little, how much
③ BOTH → a lot of, lots of, some, any, enough

💡 Much и many → в ОТРИЦАТЕЛЬНЫХ и ВОПРОСИТЕЛЬНЫХ предложениях
✗ "I have much money." → ✅ "I have a LOT OF money."
✅ "I don't have much money." / "How much money?"

⚠️ a little ≠ little:
"a little" = немного (хорошо) — "I have a little time."
"little" = почти нет (плохо) — "There is little hope." (без 'a')

exercises.text: We don't have ___ flour — we need to buy some.
I need to buy ___ eggs for the manti recipe.
exercises.hint: "eggs" = countable → "a few". "I need to buy A FEW eggs." ✅ (small positive number)

exercises.text: How ___ water should I add to the dough?
Choose the correct sentence about rice.
opts: I have a lot of rice.
exercises.correct: I have a lot of rice.
exercises.hint: "rice" = uncountable. In POSITIVE sentences → "a lot of". "I have A LOT OF rice." ✅ (not "much" in positive)

exercises.text: Do you have ___ potatoes in the fridge?
exercises.hint: "any" = questions and negative sentences. "Do you have ANY potatoes?" ✅

exercises.instruction: Complete with "a lot of", "a little", or "a few".
exercises.text: Rustam made ___ manti — enough for fifteen people.
exercises.hint: Large positive quantity → "a lot of". "Rustam made A LOT OF manti." ✅ (works for countable)

exercises.text: How ___ onions do you need for the recipe?
"There isn't any milk" is correct in a negative sentence.
exercises.hint: "any" is used in negative sentences. "There isn't ANY milk." ✅ (also: "I don't have any bread.")

exercises.instruction: Choose the correct quantifier for the positive sentence.
exercises.text: "I have ___ money left — enough for coffee." (small amount)
exercises.hint: "money" = uncountable. Small positive amount → "a little". "I have A LITTLE money left." ✅

exercises.text: She added ___ tablespoons of oil to the filling.
"How many water did you add?" — What is wrong?
exercises.hint: ✅ "How MUCH water did you add?" — "water" is uncountable → "much" ✅

questions.hint: "flour" is uncountable — you can't say "one flour, two flours". → "How MUCH flour?"
"eggs" is countable — one egg, two eggs. → "How MANY eggs?"
Positive sentence + uncountable → "a lot of". "I have A LOT OF rice." ✅ (not "much" in positive)

questions.text: "We don't have ___ (countable) apples — only two left."
questions.hint: "apples" = countable → "not many". "We don't have MANY apples." ✅
"salt" = uncountable. Small positive amount → "a little". "Add A LITTLE salt." ✅
"friends" = countable. Small positive number → "a few". "I have A FEW friends." ✅

questions.text: "I have much money" is correct in a positive statement.
questions.hint: In positive statements: "I have A LOT OF money." "Much" is mainly for negatives/questions. ✅

questions.text: "___ of" can be used with both countable and uncountable nouns.
questions.hint: "a lot of" works with BOTH: "a lot of eggs" (C) / "a lot of flour" (UC) ✅
"any" = questions (and negatives). "Do you have ANY milk?" ✅
"some" is used in offers and polite requests. "Would you like SOME tea?" ✅

questions.text: "___ few students attended." (almost none — negative meaning)
questions.hint: "few" WITHOUT "a" = almost none (negative meaning). "Few students came." ≠ "A few students came." ✅

questions.text: "___ little money remains." (negative meaning — almost none)
questions.hint: "little" without "a" = almost none (negative). "Little money remains." = very little, nearly nothing.

questions.text: Which is correct for a large quantity of bread?
questions.hint: "bread" = uncountable. Positive large amount → "a lot of bread." ✅ ("breads" doesn't exist)
"lots of" = "a lot of" — same meaning, slightly more informal. "lots of eggs / flour" ✅
"a lot of vegetables" = large positive amount, countable noun. ✅ Others: "much flour" (UC, not positive), "how many eggs" (C), "a lot of water" (positive, not "much").
